# The Drumback (*Pressoterra gravigrada*)

## The World It Lives In

The Drumback's home is a dense, iron-rich super-Earth where everything weighs ten times what it would on Earth. The strong gravity holds onto a thick atmosphere, about eight times as dense as ours, so the air feels almost syrupy. Mountains can't grow tall before their own weight crumbles them, so the landscape is mostly broad plains, low mesas, and shallow, wind-scoured basins. Plants grow as thick mats and crusts rather than trees. Nothing here stands tall, and nothing falls without consequence. A drop of 10 centimeters hits as hard as a one-meter fall on Earth.

## Body Plan

**Size and shape:** An adult Drumback is about 1.5 meters long, 1 meter wide, and only 25 centimeters tall at its highest point. From above it looks like an oval paving stone or a flattened tortoise. A low profile matters: the taller an animal is, the farther it can fall and the harder its heart must pump to push blood upward.

**Limbs:** It has **twelve short legs** in six pairs, splayed slightly outward like a lizard's but much thicker. Each leg is barely longer than it is wide, a stout column ending in a broad, padded foot. Spreading the weight across many legs means no single limb carries a crushing load. When the animal rests, it lowers its belly onto the ground and lets its whole underside bear the weight, like a beached seal.

**Skeleton:** Its bones are dense, solid, and laced with mineral deposits similar to iron oxide, which makes them heavier but far stronger under compression. The spine isn't a single chain of vertebrae. It is a **lattice of interlocking plates**, more like a woven basket than a column, so loads spread across the whole torso. The upper shell, the "drum," is a domed carapace. Its arch shape carries weight efficiently and protects against falling debris.

## Internal Systems

**Circulation:** A single heart couldn't handle the pressure differences in a 10g environment, so the Drumback has **six small hearts** arranged in a ring around its body. They beat in a rolling sequence, like a wave. The animal is so flat that blood never has to climb more than a few centimeters, but the distributed pumps keep pressure even when it tilts over uneven ground. Its blood vessels have thick, muscular walls, and valves in every vein stop blood from pooling in the lower body.

**Breathing:** Because the air is so dense, each breath carries far more oxygen than on Earth. Its lungs are surprisingly small: flat, sheet-like sacs under the carapace that it fills by gently flexing its shell plates. It breathes slowly, only three or four times a minute.

**Metabolism:** Moving anything in 10g is expensive, so the Drumback is built for **efficiency over speed**. It walks at about half a kilometer per hour, but it can keep going almost indefinitely. Its muscles are mostly slow-twitch, dense, and fatigue-resistant, made for endurance and steady force rather than bursts.

## Senses

**Seismic hearing:** The Drumback's most important sense is in its feet. Each of its twelve footpads contains vibration-sensing organs that pick up tremors through the ground. Comparing tiny timing differences between its feet tells it the direction and distance of other animals, rockslides, or approaching storms.

**The drum:** Its namesake feature is a hollow resonating chamber under the carapace. By tensing muscles across its shell, it produces deep, booming pulses that travel very well through the thick air and into the ground. Drumbacks "talk" across distances of several kilometers with complex rhythmic patterns. Each individual has its own signature beat.

**Vision:** Two pairs of small, wide-set eyes sit on short, flexible stalks at the front edge of the shell. They are tuned for horizontal scanning, since most of what matters is on the same plane. A third, simpler eye-patch on top of the carapace detects shadows overhead and warns of rare dangers from above, like falling rock along mesa edges.

## Behavior and Ecology

**Diet:** It is a grazer. It shuffles across the plains scraping mineral-rich crust-plants off rocks with a broad, keratinous lower lip, much like a sea urchin's grazing apparatus but on a larger scale. It eats almost constantly.

**Danger and defense:** Its main predator is the *wedge-maw*, a flat ambush hunter that buries itself in loose sediment. Predators on this world can't chase prey. Sprinting costs too much energy, and tripping at speed could be fatal. So nearly all hunting is ambush-based. When the Drumback senses danger through its feet, it drops flat, clamps its shell edges to the ground, and anchors itself with muscular foot-suction. Prying one up is nearly impossible.

**Social life:** Drumbacks travel in loose herds of a dozen or so and coordinate through their drum signals. During storms, when dense, fast winds carry enough force to roll a careless animal, they gather into a tightly interlocked mat, shells overlapping like scales, and ride it out together.

**Reproduction:** Females give birth to two or three tiny live young, each only about 8 centimeters long. Small bodies handle high gravity far better because strength scales with cross-sectional area while weight scales with volume. For their first year the young cling to the underside of their mother's shell, protected and carried along. They eventually emerge, already shaped like miniature adults, and stay in the herd for several years.

**Lifespan:** Slow metabolism and few predators make them long-lived. Drumbacks can reach 150 years, growing slowly throughout life. The oldest are recognized by the deep, complex rhythms of their drumming, which the herd seems to follow during migrations.

## A Moment in Its Life

At dawn, a herd of Drumbacks moves across a gray-green plain of crust-moss, each animal shuffling forward at a glacial, deliberate pace. The air hums with low booms as they keep in contact. Suddenly every animal freezes and sinks flat. One elder has felt a faint, irregular tremor through its rear left feet: something shifting in the sediment ahead. A sharp double-beat ripples through the herd, and slowly, carefully, they change course. Nobody runs, because on this world nobody ever runs. They simply go around, patient as stone.

# The Shalecrawler

*A grazing animal from a world where everything weighs ten times more*

## First Impressions

If you saw a shalecrawler, you might first mistake it for a slab of weathered rock that had started moving. It is about 1.2 meters long, 50 centimeters wide, and only 8 centimeters tall at the center of its back. Its mass is about 30 kg, but on its home world it weighs what a 300 kg animal would on Earth. Its whole body plan answers one problem: **how not to be crushed by yourself.**

## Body Shape: Flat Is Survival

Gravity punishes height. Under 10g, falling just 10 cm hits you as hard as falling a full meter on Earth, so a tall animal that tripped would shatter. The shalecrawler avoids this by being pancake-flat, shaped like a cross between a trilobite and a flounder. Its center of mass sits barely 4 cm off the ground, so it essentially *cannot* fall. At worst, it tips.

Its outer edges end in a flexible, leathery skirt that can press down against the ground, sealing the animal in place like a suction cup. This is its main defense.

## Skeleton: Armored Girders

Bones under 10g have to resist not just weight but the huge forces of every step. The shalecrawler has a hybrid skeleton:

- **Dorsal plates:** Overlapping, heavily mineralized shields across the back. They act like the arched roof of a building, spreading load toward the edges.
- **Internal trusses:** Hollow, tube-shaped struts run crosswise inside the body, braced like bridge girders. Tubes give the most stiffness for the least material.
- **Dense mineralization:** Its bone incorporates iron and silicon compounds drawn from its diet, making it far denser and harder than Earth bone.

## Legs: Many, Short, and Straight

The shalecrawler has **18 pairs of stubby, pillar-like legs**, each only about 3 cm long. Several design choices follow from gravity:

- **Legs point straight down**, not sprawled out to the side like a lizard's. Sprawling creates leverage that would snap joints under this load.
- **Many legs share the weight**, so no single limb carries much.
- **Broad, padded feet** spread pressure so the animal doesn't sink into soft ground.

It moves with a rippling wave gait, legs lifting in sequence from back to front like a millipede's. It's slow, about walking pace for a human toddler, but steady. It never runs, and jumping is physically meaningless to it. It has no concept of "airborne."

## Circulation: Many Small Hearts

Blood is heavy, and pumping it uphill under 10g is brutal. Even the shalecrawler's 8 cm of height creates a pressure difference like 80 cm on Earth. So instead of one central heart, it has **a chain of six small hearts** running along its body. Each serves a local region, so no heart has to push blood far or high. Its vessels are thick-walled and packed with one-way valves to stop blood from pooling in its underside.

## Breathing: Thick Air Helps

A planet with 10g holds onto a very dense atmosphere, perhaps several times Earth's sea-level pressure. Gas exchange is easy in such air, so the shalecrawler has no lungs. Rows of **spiracles** (breathing pores) along its flanks let air diffuse into a branching network of tubes, much like insects on Earth. Insects can't grow large on Earth partly because diffusion is too slow, but the dense air here makes the system viable at this size.

## Senses: Feeling the World Through the Ground

- **Seismic sense:** Its main sense. Each foot holds vibration receptors, and the animal "listens" through the ground. Footsteps, rockfalls, and other creatures register as tremors. With 36 feet spread across its body, it can triangulate a source precisely.
- **Hearing:** Dense air carries sound powerfully, so it has membrane-covered ears on its back plates, tuned to low-frequency rumbles.
- **Vision:** It can't raise its head to look around, and eye stalks would snap. Instead, **two broad bands of compound eyes** wrap around the rim of its shell, giving nearly 360° vision of the horizon. Since nothing on this planet is tall, the horizon is where everything happens.
- **Balance organs:** Extremely sensitive statocysts detect even slight slopes. A drop-off of half a meter is a mortal danger, and the shalecrawler can sense a tilting surface long before reaching an edge.

## Diet: Grazing the Living Carpet

Plants face the same problem animals do: lifting water upward is enormously costly under 10g, so there are no trees. Vegetation grows as **dense, spongy mats**, part lichen and part moss, carpeting the flat plains in deep reds and blacks (dark pigments to absorb light filtered through the thick atmosphere).

The shalecrawler's mouth is on its underside, near the front. As it walks, a band of rasping, file-like teeth scrapes the mat beneath it, so it eats wherever it goes. It leaves behind faint pale trails, which regrow in a few weeks.

## Predators and Defense

Its main predator is the **wedgejaw**, a low, armored ambush hunter. With no pouncing possible, predators here rely on leverage. The wedgejaw shoves a flat, shovel-like snout under the edge of its prey to pry it up and flip it over, exposing the soft underside.

The shalecrawler's response is to **clamp**: it presses its skirt to the ground, creates suction, and locks its dorsal plates. A clamped adult is nearly impossible to pry loose. Since heavy gravity is on its side, the shalecrawler only has to hold still and let the planet do the work.

## Social Life and Reproduction

Shalecrawlers graze in loose herds of 10 to 40, sometimes lining up edge to edge so their skirts overlap. This creates a continuous armored surface that predators can't get under.

Females brood eggs in a chamber beneath the central shell. Hatchlings, only a few centimeters long, cling to their mother's underside for months, protected by her body and feeding on scraps from her rasping. When she clamps, they're sealed safely inside.

They communicate through **foot-drumming**, rhythmic tapping that sends vibration patterns through the ground to others up to a kilometer away.

## The Landscape It Lives In

The shalecrawler's world is profoundly flat. Mountains can't grow tall before their own weight crushes their bases, so the highest peaks are mere hills. Rain falls hard, rivers are broad and shallow, and erosion grinds everything level. A meter-high ledge is a major landmark, and a dangerous one.

**A thought experiment:** If you brought a shalecrawler to Earth, it would feel almost weightless. Its muscles would be absurdly overpowered, and a casual push of its legs might lift it clear off the ground. It would likely panic, sensing for the first time in its species' history the sensation of *falling.*

# The Slabcrawler (*Gravigrada tessellata*)

## The World It Lives On

To have 10 times Earth's surface gravity, a rocky planet would need to be large and very dense, a "super-Earth" with a heavy iron core. Its atmosphere would likely be thick, compressed into a dense layer hugging the surface. Mountains would be low and worn, because rock can't stack very high before it crushes under its own weight. The landscape would be mostly broad plains, shallow basins, and wind-scoured flats.

Everything here is shaped by one rule: **height is dangerous, and falling is deadly.** An object dropped from 30 cm hits the ground at about 7.7 m/s, the same as falling 3 meters on Earth. For a creature on this world, tripping is like falling off a roof.

---

## Overall Body Plan

The Slabcrawler looks like a living paving stone: a broad, flat, oval creature about **1.2 meters long, 80 cm wide, and only 25–30 cm tall**. It masses around 40 kg but *weighs* what a 400 kg animal would on Earth.

Its shape follows the **square-cube law**. As an animal grows, its weight increases faster than the strength of its bones and muscles. So the Slabcrawler is built low, wide, and squat, distributing its load across as much ground as possible.

### Carapace
Its back is covered by a **tessellated shell** of interlocking hexagonal plates, like a tortoise shell crossed with chain mail. The plates are slightly flexible at the seams so the body can twist without cracking. The shell isn't mainly for predators. It protects against:
- **Rain**, which falls much harder here. Raindrops reach high terminal velocities and sting like hail.
- **Falling debris**, since even a pebble rolling off a ledge strikes with real force.

### The Belly Skid
The underside is lined with thick, keratinous **skid plates**, a smooth armored sole. The Slabcrawler's body never rises far off the ground. If it stumbles, it drops only a few centimeters onto its armored belly instead of falling over.

---

## Legs and Locomotion

The Slabcrawler has **eight legs**, short and columnar like an elephant's but proportionally much thicker. Each leg is about as wide as it is long.

- **Why eight?** More legs share the load, and the animal can always keep at least five or six feet planted. It never has a "flight phase" where all feet leave the ground, because running or jumping in the human sense would be suicidal.
- **Why columnar rather than splayed?** Sprawling legs, like a lizard's, need constant muscle effort to hold the body up. Straight, pillar-like legs carry weight through the bones, which saves enormous energy at 10g.
- **Bones** are dense, heavily mineralized, and filled with a honeycomb lattice rather than hollow marrow cavities. Joints are broad, flat, and padded with thick cartilage discs.

### The Fast Shuffle
Here's a counterintuitive detail: the Slabcrawler **steps very quickly**. A swinging leg behaves like a pendulum, and pendulums swing faster in stronger gravity, roughly 3 times faster at 10g. So the Slabcrawler moves with a rapid, rippling, almost insect-like patter of short steps. Seen from a distance, it seems to glide across the ground like a slow hovercraft, its legs a blur beneath the shell edge.

Top speed is modest, maybe a brisk human walking pace. Nothing on this planet chases anything very fast.

---

## Circulation: The Problem of Blood Pressure

In strong gravity, fluids pool downward hard. On Earth, a giraffe needs extremely high blood pressure to push blood 2 meters up to its brain. At 10g, **just 20 cm of height difference is equivalent to that giraffe's neck.**

The Slabcrawler solves this in several ways:
- **Everything is level.** Its brain sits at almost exactly the same height as its main heart. It has no raised head and no neck to speak of.
- **Distributed hearts.** Besides a central heart, it has small muscular **"leg pumps"** at the top of each limb that squeeze blood back up from the feet, helped by one-way valves.
- **Tight skin and pressure sheaths.** The legs are wrapped in tough, inelastic tissue that keeps fluid from pooling, like built-in compression stockings.

If a Slabcrawler is ever flipped or tilted steeply, it can black out within seconds as blood rushes away from its brain.

---

## Senses

### Low Vision
With its eyes only about 25 cm off the ground, the Slabcrawler can't see very far over uneven terrain. It has **two rows of small, wide-angle eyes** set along the front rim of its shell, giving it nearly panoramic vision at ground level. Its sight is good for nearby motion but poor for distance.

### Hearing the Ground
Its main long-range sense is **vibration**. The dense atmosphere carries sound well, and the hard, compacted ground carries it even better. Sensitive pads on each foot pick up seismic tremors. A Slabcrawler can feel another animal's footsteps hundreds of meters away and judge its size from the rhythm.

### Smell
Dense air holds scent molecules close to the ground in thick, slow-moving layers. The Slabcrawler has **sensory pits** along the leading edge of its shell that constantly sample this low "scent fog."

---

## Feeding

Plant life on this world is also low and flat. There are no trees, only **mineral-crusted mats** resembling lichens, mosses, and leathery ground-spreading growths that hug rocks and soil.

The Slabcrawler is a grazer. Its mouth sits on the *underside* of the front of its body, like a sea urchin's or a manta ray's. It plows slowly forward, scraping up mat-growth with a **rasping, file-like tongue** reinforced with mineral teeth. Grit wears these teeth down constantly, so they continuously regrow.

It has a long, coiled gut and digests slowly. Energy is precious, since just standing up costs a lot.

---

## Predators and Defense

Predators here can't pounce, leap, or chase at high speed. Instead, they tend to:
- **Ambush** from shallow burrows.
- **Pry.** The deadliest hunters specialize in wedging under a prey animal's shell edge and **flipping it**. A flipped Slabcrawler faces disaster: it can't right itself easily, blood floods its back, and it quickly passes out.

So the Slabcrawler's main defense is to **clamp down**. When it senses danger through its feet, it pulls its legs inward, drops its armored rim flush against the ground, and uses muscular suction along the belly skid to seal itself to the surface, much like a limpet on a rock. In 10g, an animal pressed flat to the ground is extraordinarily hard to lift. Tough armor, enormous weight, and a low center of gravity make it a fortress.

---

## Life Cycle

Females dig shallow nest scrapes and lay clutches of hard, round eggs. The hatchlings, about the size of a coin, are surprisingly agile. Because of the square-cube law, **small animals are relatively much stronger than large ones.** Juveniles can scramble over rocks, climb small ledges, and move in quick bursts. They spend their youth sheltering in crevices and cracks.

As they grow, their agility steadily drains away. Climbing becomes too risky, then impossible. By adulthood they settle into the slow, flat, armored life of the plains. Elders, the largest individuals, barely move at all. They graze in slow arcs and can live for well over a century.

---

## Behavior and Social Life

Slabcrawlers gather in loose herds called **"pavements."** A herd resting together with shells touching looks like a cobblestone road stretching across the plain. Packed this way, they're even harder for predators to pry apart.

They communicate mostly through **ground-drumming**: rhythmic stamping of the feet that sends pulses through the soil. Different rhythms mean "danger," "food here," "I'm ready to mate," or simply "I'm still here." On a quiet day, the plains hum with these slow, low patterns, carried for kilometers through the dense crust.

---

## Quick Stats

| Trait | Value |
|---|---|
| Length | ~1.2 m |
| Height | ~25–30 cm |
| Mass | ~40 kg (weighs ~400 kg Earth-equivalent) |
| Legs | 8, columnar |
| Top speed | ~5 km/h |
| Diet | Grazer of ground-mat vegetation |
| Lifespan | 100+ years |
| Key danger | Being flipped over |
| Key sense | Seismic vibration through the feet |

---

The Slabcrawler is a creature built around one constant pressure: a world that is always pulling down, hard. Everything it is, flat, heavy, armored, slow, and patient, is an answer to that pull.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
# The Lowback

## The World It Lives On

To understand the Lowback, start with its world. At 10g, everything that isn't firmly attached wants to be on the ground.

- **Falling is lethal.** A 10 cm drop hits as hard as a 1 m drop on Earth. A 1 m fall is like falling off a three-story building.
- **The landscape is flat.** Mountains collapse under their own weight, so the tallest peaks are rounded hills a few hundred meters high.
- **The air is thick and stratified.** The strong gravity holds a dense atmosphere and compresses it near the ground. Air pressure drops noticeably over just a few hundred meters of elevation, so "high ground" is genuinely thin-aired and cold.
- **There are no trees.** Plant life grows as thick, rubbery mats, crusts, and low cushions, spreading outward instead of upward. Sunlight is competed for horizontally.

The Lowback grazes these mats.

## Body Plan

An adult Lowback is about **1.8 meters long, 1 meter wide, and only 25 centimeters tall**. Seen from above, it looks like a giant, armored, slightly domed flatbread. Seen from the side, it barely looks like an animal at all, more like a rock that occasionally moves.

That flatness is a matter of survival.

**Its center of gravity sits almost on the ground.** A tall animal at 10g is always one stumble away from a fatal fall. The Lowback can't really fall at all; it can only tilt.

**Its weight is spread wide.** The animal masses about 300 kg, which here means it *weighs* as much as a 3-ton object on Earth. Distributing that load over a large footprint keeps it from sinking into soft ground and from crushing its own internal organs.

## Skeleton and Legs

The Lowback has **ten legs**, five per side, and they look nothing like an Earth mammal's.

- Each leg is a **short, thick column**, barely 15 cm long, positioned directly beneath the body like the pillars of a parking garage. Sprawling, bent legs like a lizard's would need enormous muscle force just to hold the elbows in place.
- The bones are **dense, nearly solid, and stubby**. Bone strength scales with cross-sectional area while weight scales with volume, so long slender bones would snap. Its leg bones are almost as wide as they are long.
- The feet are broad, **padded discs** with a fibrous, shock-absorbing core, like a stack of tire rubber.
- The spine isn't a single column but a **flexible lattice of interlocking plates** running the width of the body. This "ribcage-spine" acts like a suspension bridge, distributing load across all ten legs so no single limb bears too much.

It walks in a **rippling wave**, lifting only two or three legs at a time and never more than a few centimeters. Most of its body is always supported. It never runs, jumps, or gallops; leaving the ground is not something any large animal on this planet does on purpose.

That said, it isn't slow. Gravity snaps each leg back down quickly, giving its gait a fast, pattering rhythm. A walking Lowback sounds like heavy rain on a tin roof.

## Circulation: The Problem of Blood

On Earth, a giraffe needs extremely high blood pressure to push blood up its neck. At 10g, every centimeter of height costs ten times as much. If a Lowback raised its head 1 meter, it would need a blood pressure of roughly **740 mmHg** just to reach its brain, about six times a healthy human's.

The Lowback's solution has three parts:

1. **It stays flat.** Its brain is never more than about 20 cm above its lowest blood vessel.
2. **It has multiple hearts.** Five small, muscular pumps run along its body in a chain, each handling a local loop. No single heart has to fight gravity across the whole animal.
3. **Its vessels are reinforced.** The veins in its lower body have thick walls and one-way valves every few centimeters, and its leg muscles squeeze blood upward with each step, so walking helps circulation.

If you forced a Lowback to stand on its end, it would lose consciousness within seconds as blood drained from its brain. Being flipped onto its side is a real emergency.

## Breathing

The dense, oxygen-rich air near the ground is easy to breathe, so the Lowback's lungs are surprisingly **small and flat**, tucked like sheets between the spine plates. It breathes through a row of **slit-like spiracles along its back edge**, which close tightly during dust storms.

Because the air is so dense, sound travels well and carries far, which shapes how it communicates.

## Senses

**Eyes:** The Lowback has two pairs of eyes. A pair of wide, horizontal-slit eyes at the front gives it a panoramic view of the flat horizon, where most threats appear. A second, smaller pair on top of its carapace watches the sky, mostly for **falling debris**. At 10g, hail, rocks dislodged from hills, and even large raindrops strike with real force. When the dorsal eyes detect something falling, the animal clamps down and lets its armor take the hit.

**Ground sense:** Its feet are packed with vibration receptors. On a dense, compacted world, the ground transmits vibration superbly, and a Lowback can feel a predator's footsteps hundreds of meters away.

**Hearing:** It hears low-frequency sound exceptionally well, through membranes along its flanks.

## Feeding

The Lowback is a **grazer that eats like a lawnmower**. Its mouth is a wide, horizontal slot on its underside at the front, lined with rows of hard, chisel-like plates. It shuffles slowly forward over the plant mats, shearing off the top layer as it goes.

The plants here are tough, fibrous, and packed with minerals, since they too must resist being flattened. The Lowback's gut is long and folded, and it carries **gastroliths**, stones it swallows to help grind tough food. On this world, swallowed stones are heavy and effective.

There's no running from danger, so the Lowback is built to endure it.

- **Armor:** Its back is covered in overlapping, slightly domed plates. The dome shape spreads impact force, the same principle as an arch.
- **The clamp:** When threatened, it pulls its legs in, drops flat, and seals the edges of its carapace against the ground with a rubbery skirt of skin. A clamped Lowback is almost impossible to pry up, since any predator would have to lift 3 Earth-tons of effective weight.
- **The flip:** Its main predator, the **Wedgejaw**, a long, low, eel-like hunter, tries to wedge its spade-shaped head under a Lowback's edge and lever it onto its side, where it will pass out from the blood shift. Lowbacks guard their edges fiercely and can shove sideways with surprising force.

## Communication and Social Life

Lowbacks live in loose herds of 10 to 30. They communicate in two ways:

- **Deep booming calls** produced by forcing air through a resonating chamber in the carapace. These carry for kilometers through the thick air.
- **Foot drumming**, which travels through the ground. A sharp, rapid drumming means "predator, clamp down." A slow rolling rhythm means "this way, good food."

At night, herds gather in tight circles, edges overlapping like shingles. This shared formation means a Wedgejaw can't find an exposed edge to get under. Young are kept in the center.

Females lay clutches of 4 to 6 **flat, leathery eggs** in shallow scrapes and lie over them, using their bodies as both incubator and shield.

Hatchlings are tiny, about the size of a human hand, and here small size is an advantage. The square-cube law is on their side: a small creature is relatively strong for its weight and survives falls that would kill an adult. Young Lowbacks are the only members of the species that can scramble over small rocks or tumble down a bank unharmed. As they grow, they gradually become more cautious, heavier, flatter, and more armored, until as adults they never willingly climb anything higher than their own body.

A Lowback herd drifts across a plain of rust-colored mat-plants under a thick, hazy sky. The animals move in a slow, pattering ripple, leaving shorn trails behind them. A low boom rolls across the herd from the leader; the ground hums faintly with answering drumming.

A few seconds later, the plates lift, ten legs on each animal unfold, and the patter resumes, as if nothing happened. On a world where everything falls hard, the Lowback has made itself into something that can't fall at all.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
# The Thrumback (*Planiterra gravissima*)

*A large grazing animal from a world where everything weighs ten times what it would on Earth*

---

## Overview

At first glance, a Thrumback looks like a boulder that has been melted and poured across the ground. It is a broad, low, dome-shaped animal about **1.8 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, but only 22 centimeters tall** at its highest point. It has a mass of about 60 kg, but under 10g it weighs what a 600 kg animal would on Earth. Nearly every feature of its body answers one problem: **how to live when height is dangerous and every movement costs ten times the effort.**

---

## Body Plan: Built Like a Bridge

**The carapace.** The Thrumback's back is a vaulted shell of layered mineral and protein, shaped like a shallow cathedral dome. An arch turns downward weight into sideways compression, which rock-like materials handle well, so the shell carries its own weight and channels it down into the legs. The underside (plastron) is flatter, made of overlapping keratin-like plates that work as skids.

**The skeleton.** Its internal bones are short, thick, and honeycombed, like bird bones but filled with a dense mineral lattice. There are no long bones anywhere. A long bone under 10g would snap or buckle, so the longest single bone in the body is about 9 cm.

**The center of gravity** sits only about 8 cm off the ground. On this planet, falling is the main cause of death for large animals. An object dropped from 1 meter here hits the ground as fast as one dropped from 10 meters on Earth. For the Thrumback, simply tipping over is a serious injury.

---

## Locomotion: Twelve Legs, Never Hurrying

The Thrumback walks on **twelve short, pillar-like legs** arranged in six pairs. Each leg is about 12 cm long and sits directly under the body, like an elephant's legs, rather than splaying out like a lizard's. Sprawled legs would put enormous twisting forces on the joints.

- **The gait is a slow ripple** that passes from back to front, like a millipede's. At least eight feet are always on the ground. The animal never has fewer than three points of support on each side.
- **Top speed is about 1.5 km/h.** It never runs. Fast movement means momentum, and momentum means losing control.
- **On slopes**, it lowers its belly onto the ground and moves by "ratcheting": its skid plates grip the surface while the legs push it forward a few centimeters at a time.
- **It cannot jump**, and it has no ancestors that could. Nothing on this planet jumps except a few millimeter-sized insects.

**Feet** are broad, padded discs full of vibration-sensing cells. They are also the animal's primary sense organs (see below).

---

## Circulation: The Problem of Heavy Blood

On Earth, a giraffe needs enormous blood pressure to push blood up its neck. Under 10g, a column of blood just 10 cm tall exerts the same pressure as a 1-meter column on Earth. The Thrumback solves this in three ways:

1. **Nothing important is high up.** The brain, heart, and lungs all sit at the same level, in a horizontal band through the middle of the body.
2. **Three hearts.** A large central heart is assisted by two smaller "booster" hearts near the front and back. This keeps pressure even across the long, flat body.
3. **Leg pumps.** Blood naturally pools in the feet, so each leg is wrapped in a tight, elastic sheath with one-way valves. Every step squeezes blood back up into the body, like the calf-muscle pump in human legs, but far more developed.

---

## Breathing

The atmosphere is thick, around 20 times Earth's surface pressure, because a strong gravity well holds onto gas. Dense air carries plenty of oxygen per breath, so the lungs are relatively small.

But expanding a chest means lifting your own crushing weight. So the Thrumback doesn't breathe by raising its back. Instead, **internal muscular diaphragms slide horizontally** like pistons, pulling air in through slit-like vents along both sides of the shell. You can see a Thrumback breathing by the slow flutter of these side gills, while the dome itself never moves.

---

## Senses: Listening Through the Ground

Height means vision. A creature 22 cm tall can't see far, and the thick, hazy atmosphere scatters light into a dim amber glow anyway. So the Thrumback relies on other senses:

- **Seismic sense (primary).** All twelve feet detect ground vibrations. By comparing when a tremor reaches each foot, the animal can locate the source very precisely. It "hears" approaching predators, the footsteps of its herd, and even distant rockslides.
- **Eyes (secondary).** Two wide, horizontal eyes run along the front rim of the shell. They are good at detecting motion along the horizon and nearly useless for looking up. There is rarely anything up there worth seeing.
- **Edge whiskers.** Two stiff, sweeping feelers on the front rim constantly brush the ground ahead, checking for drop-offs. A Thrumback that detects a ledge even 20 cm deep will stop and turn. Its "fear of heights" is extremely strong and is triggered by depths a human would step over without noticing.

---

## Communication: The Thrum

The creature gets its name from its voice. It doesn't call through the air. It **drums its plastron against the ground** in deep, rhythmic pulses. Dense, flat bedrock carries these vibrations for kilometers. Herds coordinate through overlapping thrum patterns, and an alarm-thrum can spread across a whole plain in minutes as each animal relays it.

To a human visitor with bare feet, a Thrumback herd would feel like a distant, slow heartbeat coming up through the soil.

---

## Feeding

The landscape is a world of low things. Plants can't grow tall. Mountains are low and worn down, and vegetation is a rubbery, photosynthetic carpet only a few centimeters thick, spreading across the flat plains like moss.

The Thrumback's mouth is on its **underside, near the front**. It is a wide, rasping slot lined with self-replacing mineral teeth. The animal grazes by slowly gliding over the plant-carpet and scraping it up, leaving pale, mowed trails behind it. Food never has to be lifted. Swallowing moves horizontally.

---

## Predators and Defense

Its main predator is the **wedgeback**, a flat, low-slung ambush hunter that lies buried in sediment. Its jaws are shaped like a pry bar. Its strategy is to slip its wedge under the rim of a Thrumback's shell and lever it up, exposing the soft underside. Flipping one over completely is a death sentence, because a Thrumback on its back can rarely right itself.

The Thrumback's defense is to **clamp down.** At the first alarm, it drops its body, pulls in its legs, and presses a flexible muscular skirt around the shell rim tight against the ground, sealing itself like a limpet. Combined with its huge effective weight, this creates a suction seal that is almost impossible to pry loose. A clamped Thrumback can wait out a predator for hours.

---

## Reproduction and Life Cycle

Thrumbacks lay flat, leathery, disc-shaped eggs in shallow scraped hollows. The hatchlings show something interesting about life under high gravity: **small creatures handle gravity far better than large ones.** This follows from the square-cube law, since strength scales with cross-section while weight scales with volume.

So juveniles, about the size of a human hand, are surprisingly agile. They scurry, climb over pebbles, and can even survive small tumbles. As they grow, they become steadily more cautious, slower, and flatter. An adult Thrumback can no longer do things it did casually as a juvenile. Their behavior changes along with their body. The young explore, and the old stay put.

Adults can live for over 150 years. Their low metabolism suits a life spent mostly resting belly-down, where holding still costs almost nothing.

---

## A Day in the Life

At dawn, a herd of thirty Thrumbacks lies flat in a loose cluster, looking like a field of stones. The first thrums pass between them, slow and low. One by one they rise a few centimeters on their twelve legs and begin to ripple forward, scraping pale paths through the amber plant-carpet. Juveniles dart between them. When one adult's edge whiskers find a shallow crack in the bedrock, the whole herd slowly turns to go around it. Hours later, a deep, sharp thrum spreads through the ground. Instantly, thirty shells clamp flat, and the plain falls silent until the wedgeback gives up and moves on.

---

**In short:** the Thrumback is what happens when evolution treats height as the enemy. It is flat, slow, many-legged, ground-listening, and built like an arch. Every part of it is designed so that it never has to fall.

# The Pavisk

*A grazing animal from a world with ten times Earth's gravity*

---

## The World It Lives On

To understand the Pavisk, you first have to understand its home. A planet with 10g surface gravity would be strange in ways that ripple through everything:

- **The atmosphere is crushingly dense** but hugs the ground in a thin layer. Air pressure might be dozens of times Earth's, and the air behaves almost like a thin fluid.
- **The terrain is flat.** Mountains collapse under their own weight, so the tallest peaks are worn-down ridges a few hundred meters high. Most of the world is plains, low mesas, and shallow, fast-rippling seas.
- **Falling is the great killer.** An object falling from just 10 cm hits the ground as hard as one falling 1 meter on Earth. A 1-meter fall there is like falling 10 meters here.

Every feature of the Pavisk is an answer to one question: *how do you stay alive when the ground is always trying to kill you?*

---

## Body Plan

**Size:** About 60 cm long, 40 cm wide, and only 8 cm tall at its highest point. It weighs around 6 kg in mass, but on its world that feels like 60 kg of load on its frame.

**Shape:** It looks like a living paving stone, or an overturned shallow bowl. The body is a broad, flattened oval with a gently domed back. Its center of gravity sits barely 3 cm off the ground. It is almost impossible to tip over, which, as we'll see, is the whole point.

**Coloring:** Mottled grey-brown with darker radial streaks, matching the gravel plains where it grazes. From above, a resting Pavisk is nearly indistinguishable from a flat rock.

---

## Skeleton and Support

On Earth, the strength of a bone depends on its cross-sectional area, while weight scales with volume. This is the **square-cube law**, and at 10g it is brutal.

- **Bones** are short, wide, and almost solid. There is very little marrow cavity. They are reinforced with layered mineral deposits that may include silica as well as calcium compounds, making them closer to ceramic composite than to our bones.
- **The spine** is a broad, flexible plate of interlocking segments rather than a column. It works like a suspension bridge, spreading load across the whole body.
- **The underside** has a tough, keratinous belly-plate. When the Pavisk rests, it doesn't lie down so much as *settle*, letting the belly take the weight and giving its legs a break.

---

## Legs and Movement

The Pavisk has **ten legs**, five down each side.

- Each leg is short and thick, built like a pillar rather than a lever. The legs are positioned almost directly beneath the body, because sprawling legs (like a lizard's) would need enormous muscle effort just to hold the body up.
- **It never has fewer than six feet on the ground.** Its gait is a slow, rippling wave that passes from back to front, like a millipede in slow motion. It cannot run, and it never, ever jumps.
- **The feet** are wide, padded discs ringed with short, hooked claws that grip the ground. On slopes, it presses its whole belly down and pulls itself along.
- **Top speed** is perhaps 1 meter per second in short bursts. Its normal pace is a deliberate creep.

A Pavisk that trips is in real danger. A leg that buckles could drop part of its body a few centimeters, enough to crack a rib-plate. So it moves with constant, careful contact, testing each step.

---

## Circulation: The Blood Pressure Problem

On Earth, a giraffe needs enormous blood pressure to push blood up its neck. At 10g, even a few centimeters of height difference creates a serious pressure gradient. A 10 cm column of blood at 10g has the same pressure difference as a 1-meter column on Earth.

The Pavisk's solutions:

- **It keeps everything level.** Its head is never more than a few centimeters above or below its heart. It cannot raise its head to look around. Evolution has simply forbidden it.
- **It has multiple hearts.** A main heart sits in the center of the body, with smaller booster hearts near the head and along each flank, so no single pump has to fight gravity over a long distance.
- **Its vessels are thick-walled and valved** throughout, like the veins in our legs but everywhere. This prevents blood from pooling in the lowest parts of the body.

---

## Breathing

The dense atmosphere is actually a gift. With so many gas molecules packed into each breath, oxygen exchange is easy.

- The Pavisk has **small, stiff lungs** that don't need to expand much. They are ventilated by a pumping action of the belly-plate against the body wall.
- Breathing slits run along both sides of the body, just above the leg line, so it can breathe even when pressed flat to the ground.
- Its breaths are slow and shallow. A resting Pavisk takes perhaps one breath every 20 seconds.

---

## Senses

**Vision:** On a flat world with a low horizon, the useful information is almost all at ground level. The Pavisk has a **continuous band of simple eyes** running around the rim of its body, giving it full 360° vision in a narrow horizontal strip. It sees almost nothing above it, but very little threat comes from above on a world where flight is nearly impossible.

**Hearing:** Sound travels powerfully through dense air. The Pavisk hears through membranes on its back that are sensitive to very low frequencies. It can detect another creature's movement from hundreds of meters away.

**Ground sense:** Its feet are packed with vibration-sensitive nerves. It feels footsteps through the soil the way a spider feels its web.

---

## Feeding

The Pavisk is a grazer. The plants of its world are themselves low and flat: mats, crusts, and creeping rosettes pressed against the ground, since anything tall would collapse or be torn apart by the dense, powerful winds.

- Its mouth is on the **underside of the front rim**. It feeds by creeping slowly over plant mats and scraping them with a rasping, file-like tongue, a bit like a giant snail.
- A grazing herd leaves behind pale, scraped trails across the dark plant-crust, visible from a distance as long, winding stripes.

---

## Predators and Defense

Here's where the 10g world gets truly strange. Most predators on Earth kill with teeth and claws. On the Pavisk's world, the deadliest weapon is **gravity itself**.

**The main predator** is a creature called the *Lever-jaw*: a long, low hunter with a wedge-shaped head. It doesn't try to bite through the Pavisk's armored back. Instead, it jams its head under the rim of the Pavisk and **heaves upward**, trying to flip it over or lift one side. If it can lift a Pavisk even 15 cm and let it drop, the impact can break bones and rupture organs.

**The Pavisk's defenses:**

- **Clamping:** When threatened, it drops its belly flat and digs all ten sets of claws into the ground. A clamped Pavisk can be nearly impossible to pry loose.
- **Rim armor:** The edge of its shell is reinforced and slightly flared downward, so there is no gap to wedge under. A healthy Pavisk can press its rim right into the soil.
- **Herding:** Groups of Pavisks press together edge-to-edge, forming a continuous armored pavement with no rims exposed except at the outer border.
- **Self-righting:** If flipped, a Pavisk is in grave danger, but it has one chance. It arches its flexible spine-plate and rolls using a ridge along one side of its back. Many die before they manage it.

---

## Reproduction and Life Cycle

- The Pavisk gives **live birth** to one or two young at a time. Eggs would need thick shells to survive the weight of the parent and the environment, and live birth avoids that cost.
- Newborns are tiny, about 5 cm long, and almost paper-flat. They spend their first weeks **clinging to the underside of the mother**, sheltered in a shallow groove in her belly-plate. She moves even more slowly during this time.
- Being small is actually safer at 10g, since small bodies are relatively stronger. Young Pavisks are surprisingly sturdy. The danger grows as they get bigger.
- They mature slowly and may live for decades, since their low-energy lifestyle produces little wear.

---

## Behavior and Social Life

- Pavisks live in loose herds of 10 to 40 and communicate with **deep, rumbling calls** that travel far through the dense air. Some calls are below human hearing range.
- They are extremely cautious. Ledges are deadly, so they avoid any terrain with drops greater than a few centimeters. A ditch that a human would step over without thinking is a cliff to a Pavisk.
- During violent windstorms, which carry immense force in the dense atmosphere, the whole herd clamps down together and waits, sometimes for days.

---

## The Big Picture

If you stood on the Pavisk's world (briefly, before your own skeleton failed), you would see a vast, flat plain under a heavy, hazy sky, crusted with dark plant-mats. Scattered across it would be what look like smooth grey stones. Only if you watched patiently would you notice that some of them are moving, in slow rippling waves, scraping pale trails across the ground and rumbling softly to each other in voices you could feel in your chest.

It's an animal shaped entirely by one rule: **never fall, never tip, never rise.**

# The Slabwalker

*A grazing animal from a world where gravity pulls ten times harder than on Earth*

---

## The World It Lives On

Surface gravity depends on a planet's density and radius, so a 10g world would likely be a large, iron-rich super-Earth. Its gravity holds a thick, dense atmosphere, and its landscape is strikingly flat because rock can't support tall mountains. Cliffs are rare and short, and the terrain looks like rolling plains and low terraces. This matters, because on this planet **height is death**.

A fall of 1 meter here hits as hard as a 10-meter fall on Earth, about 50 km/h at impact. Every adaptation of the Slabwalker comes back to one rule: *stay low, stay supported, never fall.*

---

## Body Plan

**Size:** About 70 cm long, 35 cm wide, and only 10 cm tall. It masses roughly 12 kg but feels the strain of carrying 120.

**Shape:** A flattened oval, like a thick paving stone with rounded edges. Its belly rides 2 to 3 cm off the ground. This is a consequence of the **square-cube law**: a limb's strength grows with its cross-sectional area, while body weight grows with volume. Tall animals become impossibly heavy for their legs, so evolution here favors wide, flat, close-to-the-ground bodies.

**Legs:** Ten short, thick, pillar-like legs sit directly beneath the body rather than splayed out to the sides. Splayed legs, like a lizard's, need constant muscular effort to keep the body up. Pillars stack bone on bone, like an elephant's legs. Each leg ends in a broad, padded foot that spreads the load and keeps the animal from sinking into soft ground.

**Gait:** The Slabwalker moves in a slow "wave gait," with ripples traveling front to back along each side. At least seven feet touch the ground at all times. It cannot run, gallop, or jump. A jump would only carry it a few centimeters, and the landing would cost more than the leap gained.

Strong gravity does make its short legs swing faster, like a pendulum on a shorter, stiffer string. As a result, the Slabwalker walks at a surprisingly brisk pace for its size, roughly as fast as a human stroll.

---

## Skeleton and Belly

The bones are dense and thick-walled, with almost no hollow space. Muscle makes up nearly 60% of the body mass, compared with about 40% in humans.

Its underside is covered in **keratin skid plates**, overlapping scales like the runners of a sled. When it rests, it simply lets its legs fold and drops onto its belly. This "slumping" is its version of sitting down, and it spends most of its time this way, because standing is expensive.

---

## Circulation: The Problem of Height

On Earth, a giraffe needs extremely high blood pressure to push blood up its neck. At 10g, even lifting blood 20 cm is like lifting it 2 meters on Earth. The Slabwalker solves this in three ways:

- **No neck.** The head is fused into the front of the body.
- **Five small hearts** spaced along the body, each pumping a short loop, instead of one large heart serving everything.
- **Valved veins throughout**, so blood can't pool in the legs.

Even so, the Slabwalker never raises its front end more than a few centimeters. When curious, it does the opposite of an Earth animal: it **flattens and spreads out** to "look" farther.

---

## Internal Organs

Organs left loose would sag and crush whatever lies beneath them. The Slabwalker's body cavity is divided into compartments by tough membranes that cradle each organ in its own hammock.

The lungs sit along the *top* of the body, braced by a rigid arch of ribs, so the animal's own weight never squeezes them. It breathes with bellows-like muscles along its sides. Because the air is so dense, each breath carries plenty of oxygen, and the lungs can be fairly small.

---

## Senses

- **Eyes:** Four eyes. Two wide-set eyes on the front edge scan the horizon, and two on the top watch for the shadow of anything overhead. Vision is tuned for a flat, horizontal world, with sharp detail along the horizon line and blurry everywhere else.
- **Seismic sensing:** Each footpad holds pressure-sensitive nerves. In high gravity, everything presses hard into the ground, so footsteps travel well through soil. A Slabwalker can feel a predator's approach long before seeing it.
- **Hearing:** Dense air carries sound efficiently, and herds communicate with deep, rumbling drones produced by vibrating the dorsal plates.

---

## Diet and Feeding

Plants on this world grow as tough, low mats and crusts, a bit like lichens or turf. A tree would collapse under its own weight. The Slabwalker's mouth sits on the front underside. It has a rasping, file-like tongue that scrapes up vegetation as the animal slides forward, like a living lawn-mower moving across the plains.

---

## Life Cycle: Agile Young, Ponderous Adults

The square-cube law has a curious effect on growth. **Small bodies are relatively strong**, because their strength-to-weight ratio is much better. Newborn Slabwalkers, only 8 cm long, are quick and nimble. They can scramble over pebbles, climb short ledges, and even make tiny hops.

As they grow, they slowly lose this agility. Adults that try juvenile tricks tend to break legs. Young are born live and ride in a shallow brood groove on the parent's back, where they're protected from being stepped on by the herd.

---

## Predators

The main threat is the **Lurkmaw**, an ambush predator even flatter than its prey. It buries itself in the turf with only its eyes exposed. Pouncing is impossible in 10g, so it attacks *horizontally*: it fires a muscular, harpoon-like tongue along the ground to snag a Slabwalker's leg, then drags the prey toward its jaws.

The Slabwalker's defense is to **clamp down**. It drops onto its belly, braces all ten legs outward, and presses its armored edge into the soil. In this gravity, a flattened 12 kg animal is enormously hard to lift or flip.

---

## Summary

The Slabwalker is what life looks like when gravity is the dominant force in every decision: flat, many-legged, multi-hearted, built from dense bone and heavy muscle, and deeply cautious. In its world, the greatest danger isn't being caught. It's being lifted, tipped, or carried over an edge.

## The World It Lives On

To reach 10 g, a rocky planet must be both larger and denser than Earth, perhaps an iron-rich super-Earth. That gravity shapes everything:

- **The atmosphere is thick and heavy**, many times Earth's surface pressure, and hazy.
- **Mountains can't grow tall.** Rock crumbles under its own weight, so the landscape is a vast expanse of low plateaus, gentle ridges, and gravel plains.
- **Falling is catastrophic.** An object dropped from knee height on Earth hits the ground here as hard as one dropped from a second-story window. Rain and hail strike like gravel.
- **Plants are flat.** The dominant vegetation is a crust of rubbery, lichen-like mats and low domes, with nothing resembling a tree.

The Pavestrider is the planet's most common large grazer, the ecological equivalent of a cow or a bison.

## Body Plan

**Size and shape:** An adult is about 1.4 meters long, 90 cm wide, and only **20 cm tall**. It looks like a living paving stone or a giant armored pancake. It has roughly the mass of a large dog (about 80 kg), but here that mass *weighs* as much as a small car.

**Why so flat?** Every centimeter of height is a liability. Height means a longer fall when the animal trips, a taller column of blood for the heart to push upward, and more leverage for its own weight to snap its limbs. Evolution squashed it.

**The skeleton:** The spine is not a rod but a **vaulted arch**, like a stone bridge, with ribs that curve down to meet a dense ventral plate. The whole frame works in compression, the way cathedrals do. Its bones are laced with mineral fibers, making them heavier but far stronger than ours.

## Legs and Movement

The Pavestrider has **ten pairs of short, columnar legs**, each about as thick as it is long. They sit directly beneath the body, like table legs, rather than sprawling out to the side like a lizard's. A sprawling posture would demand enormous muscle force just to hold the body up.

- **It never runs.** No gait ever lifts all its feet off the ground. It moves in a continuous **ripple gait**, with waves of legs stepping in sequence like a millipede's, so at least two-thirds of its feet always bear weight.
- **Top speed** is about a brisk human walking pace. It can sustain that for hours.
- **Each leg segment has its own nerve cluster.** In 10 g, a stumble becomes a fall in hundredths of a second, too fast for signals to reach a central brain and return. Local reflexes catch slips instantly.
- **The feet are broad and padded** with fibrous cushions to spread the load and absorb shock.

## Circulation

On Earth, a giraffe needs extraordinary blood pressure to reach its brain. At 10 g, even a 20 cm height difference is a serious hydraulic challenge. The Pavestrider solves this in three ways:

1. **Multiple hearts.** It has six small hearts spaced along its body, each pumping only a short local loop.
2. **A centralized brain.** It has no raised head. The brain sits in the middle of the body, at the same height as everything else, inside the strongest part of the arch.
3. **Valved vessels** throughout, like the veins in our legs, prevent blood from pooling in the feet.

The dense atmosphere packs a lot of oxygen into every breath, so the Pavestrider's lungs are small. It breathes through **rows of slit-like vents along its flanks**, which can clamp shut during dust storms. Moving thick, heavy air takes muscular effort, so its breathing is slow and deep, about four breaths a minute.

## Armor and Defense

The upper surface is covered in **overlapping domed plates**, tough enough to shrug off hailstones that hit like slingshot pellets. The plates are dark and mottled to match the gravel plains.

Its main predator is the **Flipper-jaw**, a low, wedge-shaped ambusher. In this world nothing can pounce, because leaping is suicidal. Instead, the Flipper-jaw slides its shovel-like snout under the edge of its prey and tries to **lever it onto its back**. An overturned Pavestrider, with its legs in the air and its body pressing down on its own lungs and armor at ten times its normal weight, suffocates within minutes.

So the Pavestrider's chief defense is **clamping**. When threatened, it drops flat and seals a muscular skirt around its perimeter against the ground, like a limpet on a rock. A clamped adult is nearly impossible to pry loose.

## Feeding

Its mouth is on the **underside**, near the front: a wide slot lined with a rasping, file-like plate. The Pavestrider grazes the way a sea urchin or chiton does, simply walking over the mat-vegetation and scraping it up as it goes. A herd leaves long, pale stripes across the landscape where they've fed.

## Senses

- **Vision:** Two clusters of eyes sit on low turrets at the front corners, plus a ring of simple light-sensing spots around the rim. Because nothing on this planet stands tall, line-of-sight is short and low, and the thick, hazy air blurs distance anyway. Vision matters less than it does for Earth animals.
- **Ground-sensing:** Its most important sense. Every foot is packed with vibration receptors. Dense rock carries seismic signals well, and a Pavestrider can feel a Flipper-jaw shifting its weight thirty meters away.
- **Hearing:** Thick air carries low-frequency sound very efficiently. Herds communicate with **deep infrasonic hums**, produced by vibrating the body arch, that travel for kilometers.

## Social Life and Reproduction

Pavestriders live in loose herds of 20 to 60 that drift across the plains like a slow tide. When a predator is detected, a warning rumble passes through the herd and every animal clamps down at once, turning the herd into a field of immovable stones.

Instead of laying eggs (which would need extremely thick shells), females carry developing young in a **brood chamber beneath the body arch**, the most protected space they have. Calves are born already flat and armored and walk within an hour. For their first months they travel tucked underneath their mother, emerging only to graze in her shadow.

## A Moment in Its Life

At dawn, under a dim orange sky, the herd begins to move. Hundreds of legs ripple in unison with a sound like rain on gravel. A hailstorm rolls in, and the animals simply stop, hunched under their plates, as ice cracks off their backs like thrown stones. Afterward, one young Pavestrider feels a faint, wrong vibration in its forefeet. It hums. Within two seconds, the entire herd is clamped to the earth, and somewhere nearby, a Flipper-jaw that was creeping forward on its belly goes still and waits for a mistake that never comes.

# The Crustback (*Planoderma gravis*)

The crustback is a mid-sized grazer from a world whose surface gravity is ten times Earth's. Every feature of its body answers one question: how do you stay alive when everything weighs ten times more and every fall is deadly?

---

## Basic Profile

- **Length:** ~90 cm
- **Width:** ~40 cm
- **Height:** never more than 8 cm
- **Mass:** ~6 kg, which weighs what a 60 kg animal does on Earth
- **Speed:** ~0.5 m/s at full exertion

From above, it looks like a cross between a tortoise, a chiton, and a centipede: a broad, low, oval dome edged with a skirt of overlapping plates, gliding over the ground on dozens of hidden legs.

---

## Body Plan: Flat Is Survival

**The square-cube law dominates everything.** Weight rises with volume, but bone and muscle strength rise only with cross-sectional area. Tall, slender bodies buckle. So the crustback is built like a paving stone. Its center of mass sits about 3 cm off the ground.

**Height is also dangerous.** A 10 cm fall here hits as hard as a 1 m fall on Earth. A 1 m fall equals a 10 m fall on Earth. Keeping low means the creature can never really "fall" at all.

**The arched shell.** Its dorsal carapace is a shallow vault of layered mineral and protein fibers, like nacre reinforced with something like chitin. Arches carry load through compression, which is what mineralized materials handle best. The shell isn't just armor. It's the main load-bearing frame, transferring weight down to the legs along its edges.

**It rights itself automatically.** The dome is shaped like a *gömböc*, a form with only one stable resting position. If a predator manages to flip it, the crustback simply rocks back onto its belly. This matters because an overturned animal here could never lift its own body weight to recover.

---

## Locomotion: Never Leave the Ground

**Twenty-four pairs of short, columnar legs** sit directly beneath the body, not sprawled out to the sides like a lizard's. Vertical pillars carry weight through compression with little muscular effort. Sprawled legs would demand enormous torque just to hold the body up.

**It moves by metachronal waves.** Ripples pass down the leg rows, as in a millipede, so at any moment about 80% of the feet are planted. There is no gait with an airborne phase. Running, hopping, and jumping simply don't exist in its evolutionary vocabulary.

**It rests by lying down.** When stationary, the crustback lowers its belly onto a tough, ridged sole and lets its legs go slack. Standing is metabolically expensive here, so the animal spends most of its life lying flat and rising only a few centimeters to move.

**Its edges are cautious.** The rim of the shell bristles with sensory whiskers that constantly probe for drop-offs. A crustback encountering a 20 cm ledge treats it the way you'd treat a cliff. It reroutes, sometimes for hundreds of meters.

---

## Circulation: Fighting Hydrostatic Pressure

On a 10g world, blood pressure in a vertical column rises ten times faster with height than it does on Earth. A giraffe here would be physically impossible.

- **Low height** keeps the pressure gradient across the body tiny.
- **Seven small segmental hearts** run along the body instead of one large one. Each boosts flow locally, so no single pump has to push blood far.
- **The brain sits low and central,** level with the hearts, never perched on a raised head.

---

## Breathing and the Atmosphere

High gravity holds onto gases well, so the planet has a thick atmosphere of roughly 8 Earth atmospheres. Oxygen is plentiful at that pressure, so the crustback has small, efficient lungs fed by rows of slit-like spiracles along its flanks.

The dense air also carries heat away well, so overheating is rarely an issue. And it carries **sound** extremely well, which shapes how the crustback communicates.

---

## Senses

**Eyes in a ring.** Instead of forward-facing eyes, it has a band of about 30 small eyes around the rim of its shell. Flight is rare and difficult here, so threats almost never come from above. They come along the flat horizon, and the crustback sees a full 360° panorama of it. The thick cloud cover makes days dim and amber, so its eyes are large-pupiled and sensitive to low light.

Plants on this world don't grow upward much either. The landscape is covered in **crustmats**, dense, flat, lichen-like growths a few millimeters thick, spreading across rock like living paint.

The crustback's mouth is on its underside. A rasping, tongue-like radula scrapes crustmat off the rock as it crawls, so the animal literally eats the ground it walks over. Herds leave pale, scoured trails that the mats slowly recolonize.

---

## Defense and Predators

Its main predator is the **wedgejaw**, a long, flat ambush hunter that lies buried in grit. It tries to drive a shovel-like snout under a crustback's shell edge and pry it up.

The crustback's defense is to **clamp**. It drops flat, presses its skirt plates against the ground, and uses its leg muscles to create suction along its sole. Under ten gravities of its own weight, prying one loose is brutally hard. Most attacks end with the wedgejaw giving up.

---

## Reproduction and Life Cycle

- Females lay a few flat, disc-shaped eggs and carry them in a brood chamber beneath the rear shell margin.
- Hatchlings ride under the parent's skirt for weeks, sheltered from predators and from the terrain. A young crustback never risks a fall.
- Growth is slow. Building that much structural shell takes years, and adults may live 60 to 80 Earth-years.

---

## A Day in Its Life

At dawn, the clouds glow dull orange. A herd of crustbacks lies pressed together on a broad rock plain like a scattering of dark cobblestones. One begins drumming, and the others answer. Slowly, they rise a few centimeters and ripple forward in a loose formation, rasping crustmat as they go. Their rings of eyes scan the flat horizon. When one rim-whisker touches a small ledge, the whole herd turns aside without hesitation.

Nothing hurries. Nothing jumps. On this world, being slow, flat, and patient isn't a weakness. It's the only way to live.

# The Grindle

*A grazer from the plains of a high-gravity world*

## The World It Lives On

To have ten times Earth's surface gravity, the Grindle's planet must be a dense "super-Earth," several times Earth's radius and many times its mass. That gravity shapes everything. Mountains slump under their own weight, so the landscape is a vast, nearly flat expanse of low ridges, shallow basins, and wind-polished stone. The atmosphere is crushingly thick, perhaps 15 to 20 times Earth's sea-level pressure. Rain falls fast enough to sting, and in that dense air even a moderate wind shoves like a river current.

Here, the Grindle is one of the most common large animals: a slow, armored grazer that has turned staying low into an art form.

## Body Plan: A Living Paving Stone

An adult Grindle is about **1.5 meters long, 60 centimeters wide, and only 12 centimeters tall**. From above, it looks like an oval flagstone with scalloped edges. Its shape follows from the square-cube law. On this world, height is dangerous: lifting your mass costs ten times the energy, and falling from your own height does ten times the damage. A 12 cm tumble for a Grindle is roughly like an Earth animal falling 1.2 meters, survivable but bruising. Anything taller would be fragile.

**Carapace:** The back is a mosaic of hexagonal mineralized plates joined by tough, flexible ligaments. The tiling lets the body flex over uneven ground without cracking. The plates are thick in the center and thin at the rim, keeping the center of mass as low as possible.

**Legs:** It has 22 pairs of short, columnar legs, each barely 5 cm long. They are vertical pillars that lock straight beneath the body like an elephant's, letting bone, not muscle, bear the load. They move in rippling waves down each side, like a millipede's, so that at any moment about two-thirds of the legs touch the ground. Weight is spread so evenly that the Grindle exerts less ground pressure than you might expect for such a dense animal.

**Two-sided body:** Its most unusual feature is that the Grindle has legs on *both* its top and bottom surfaces. The dorsal set is smaller and usually folded flat into grooves in the carapace. If a storm gust or a rival flips it over, it doesn't struggle to right itself, an exhausting and risky maneuver at 10g. It simply unfolds its "back" legs and walks away upside down. Its sense organs sit along the rim, so it works equally well either way up.

## Circulation and Breathing

On Earth, a giraffe needs enormous blood pressure to push blood up its neck. At 10g, even modest height differences create severe pressure gradients, which is one more reason the Grindle stays flat. Its circulatory system runs almost entirely horizontally, with **six small hearts** spaced along a central vessel. Each pumps blood a short distance to the next. No single heart has to work hard, and losing one isn't fatal.

The dense atmosphere is a gift for breathing. Each breath carries far more oxygen (or whatever oxidizer this biosphere uses) than an Earth breath. The Grindle breathes through rows of slit-like spiracles along its rim, which fan in and out slowly. It needs no large lungs, which helps keep its profile thin.

## Feeding: The Weight Mill

Grindles graze on "crustmat," a tough photosynthetic film that coats the stone plains like lichen. The Grindle's name comes from how it eats. Its entire underside is a **rasping plate** covered in rows of hard, replaceable denticles. It shuffles forward, pressing its considerable weight down, and scrapes the crustmat loose. Gravity does most of the work. Fragments are swept by tiny cilia toward a mouth slit at the front edge.

A grazing herd leaves behind pale, scoured trails in the dark crustmat, which grow back within weeks.

## Senses

**Vision:** A band of small, simple eyes rings the rim, giving 360-degree vision along the horizon. The Grindle has almost no upward vision because almost nothing threatens it from above. Flight is possible in the dense air, but only for small, light creatures with broad wings, and none are big enough to hunt a Grindle.

**Hearing and seismic sense:** Sound carries superbly through thick air and rigid bedrock. Grindles feel the ground through pressure-sensitive pads in their feet and can detect footsteps, storms, and each other from kilometers away.

**Communication:** Grindles "talk" by drumming. They raise the front of the body a few millimeters and let it drop. In 10g, even a tiny drop lands with a heavy, resonant thud. Herds coordinate movements, warn of predators, and court mates through rhythmic patterns of these thumps, which travel through the ground like low thunder.

## Behavior: Storm Pavements

The most dramatic Grindle behavior happens during the great windstorms. Air this dense, moving fast, can drag a lone animal across the plain. When the drumming signals a storm, herds gather and **lock together**. The scalloped edges of their carapaces interlock like puzzle pieces, forming a continuous living pavement that can cover hundreds of square meters. The wind flows over the smooth, unified surface, and the herd rides out the storm as a single flat mass.

Old Grindles that die inside these formations are often left in place. Over generations, their mineralized carapaces become actual pavement, patchworks of hexagonal stone that later herds return to as traditional sheltering grounds.

## Life Cycle: Agile Young, Grounded Adults

The square-cube law works differently for small creatures, so young Grindles live very different lives from their parents. Hatchlings are thumbnail-sized, relatively rounded, and surprisingly nimble. Their small mass means they can climb onto ridges, cling to rocks, and even make tiny hops that would be fatal for an adult. They spend their early lives in rock crevices, eating the soft crustmat their parents can't reach.

As they grow, their bodies become heavier relative to their strength. Gradually they flatten, their legs shorten and stiffen, and they leave the crevices for the open plains. By adulthood, a Grindle has traded agility for armor, stability, and patience. It might live for over a century, moving at a steady walk across a world where everything stays close to the ground.

## Predators

Grindles are hunted by the **wedgemaw**, a low, blade-shaped predator that slides its tapered head under a Grindle's rim and levers it upward. Lifting even one edge stresses the Grindle's body under 10g, and a predator that flips one onto a sharp ridge can crack its plates. This is the main reason Grindles evolved two-sided walking, and why a herd hit by an attack immediately drums an alarm and clamps down flat, pressing their rims to the stone so no wedge can get beneath them.

On a world where you weigh ten times what you do on Earth, the most important rule of anatomy is simple: **stay low, stay wide, and never fall.** The Slabback is a mid-sized grazing animal built around that rule.

---

An adult Slabback weighs about 40 kg, roughly the mass of a large dog, but its shape is entirely different. It's about **1.5 meters long, 80 cm wide, and only 12 cm tall** at its highest point. From above, it looks like a rounded, segmented paving stone that slowly creeps across the ground.

This shape comes straight from physics:
- **Falling is deadly.** In 10g, a 10 cm fall hits as hard as a 1-meter fall on Earth. A creature standing 1 meter tall would trip and effectively fall from a three-story building. The Slabback's low profile means even a stumble barely matters.
- **The square-cube law punishes height.** Tall structures need disproportionately thick supports. A flat, spread-out body distributes weight across many small supports instead.

## Legs & Locomotion

The Slabback has **sixteen short, columnar legs** arranged in two rows beneath its body, each only 4–5 cm long. They aren't splayed sideways like a lizard's, because that creates leverage that would snap joints under 10g. Instead they're vertical pillars, like tiny elephant legs, placing the load straight through the bone.

The legs move in **rippling waves**, like a millipede's, so at least ten are always on the ground. Things fall about three times faster here, so the natural stepping rhythm is also faster. Its legs patter in a quick, drumming cadence even though the animal itself moves at a slow walking pace.

Each foot has a thick, cushioned pad backed by a **dense, honeycombed bone** heavily mineralized for compressive strength. Its skeleton makes up nearly 30% of its body mass, compared to about 15% for a human.

## Circulation

Blood pressure is a serious problem in high gravity. On Earth, a giraffe needs enormous pressure to push blood up its neck. At 10g, a column of blood just 10 cm tall exerts the same pressure difference as a 1-meter column on Earth.

The Slabback solves this in three ways:
- **No head above the body.** Its "head" is simply the flattened front edge of its body, at exactly the same height as everything else.
- **Multiple hearts.** It has **six small hearts** spaced along its body, each serving a local region, so no single heart has to push blood far.
- **Pressure-resistant vessels.** Its veins are heavily valved and wrapped in muscle, so that every step of those sixteen legs squeezes blood back toward the hearts.

## Breathing

A planet with this much gravity holds onto a **very thick atmosphere**, perhaps several times Earth's surface pressure. That's good news for the Slabback: each breath carries far more oxygen. It breathes through **rows of slit-like spiracles** along its sides, ventilated by rhythmic contractions of its flat body, rather than lifting a heavy ribcage against gravity.

## Senses

**Vision:** A ring of small, dark eyes runs around the entire rim of its body, like the eyes on a scallop's shell. They look **horizontally**, because in this world almost everything that matters moves sideways along the ground. Anything coming from above is either already falling too fast to dodge or isn't a threat.

**Edge-sensing whiskers:** Its most vital sense organ is a fringe of stiff, sensitive bristles around its rim. They constantly sweep the ground ahead, and if they detect a drop of even a few centimeters, the animal stops instantly. A ledge 30 cm high is, to a Slabback, a lethal cliff.

**Ground hearing:** The dense air and the compressed, rocky crust carry sound and vibration extremely well. The Slabback "hears" largely through its feet, detecting the footfalls of predators and the low-frequency calls of others of its kind through the ground.

## Diet & Feeding

Plant life here grows as **low, tough, crusty mats**, like lichens or stromatolites. Tall stems are too costly to build. The Slabback feeds through a **broad, rasping mouth on its underside**, crawling over these mats and scraping them like a giant snail or a chiton. It's always grazing, and from above you'd see trails of scraped rock behind it.

## Defense & Predators

Its back is covered in **overlapping mineralized plates**, both armor and structural support. Flipping a 40 kg animal in 10g takes effectively 400 kg of force, so predators can't roll it over to reach its soft underside.

Instead, its main predator, a low, wedge-shaped hunter, works at the edges. It tries to **wedge its flat snout under the Slabback's rim** and pry or bite into the leg area. The Slabback's defense is to **clamp down**: it pulls its legs in and seals its armored rim flat against the rock like a limpet. A clamped Slabback is nearly impossible to dislodge.

Pouncing barely exists here. Jumps reach only one-tenth of their Earth height, so all hunting is ambush and grappling, a slow, grinding contest of leverage rather than speed.

## Life Cycle: The Agile Young

One of the most striking features of the Slabback is how different its babies are.

Newborns are only a few centimeters across. Because of the square-cube law, small creatures are much stronger relative to their weight, so **juveniles are quick, nimble, and even able to climb** small rocks and scramble over obstacles that would kill an adult.

As they grow, their mass increases faster than their strength. They gradually become flatter, heavier, and more cautious, eventually settling into the slow, slab-like adult form. A Slabback's life runs from a darting, adventurous childhood to a ponderous, careful adulthood, a transition forced on it entirely by gravity.

Slabbacks gather in loose herds on open rock flats, communicating with **deep, thrumming vibrations** pressed through their bodies into the ground. In storms (the dense atmosphere produces winds with tremendous force), they huddle edge to edge, forming a living pavement that sheds the wind.

They're long-lived, slow-metabolizing, and patient. They don't explore much, never take risks near edges, and treat every unfamiliar dip in the terrain with suspicion, which on a world like theirs is exactly the right attitude.
